Er Mu opens with the voice assistants we love to tease, from Siri to Xiaomi’s Xiao Ai to Alexa, and with fictions such as the film Her and the Japanese drama Your Turn to Kill, whose widowed hero keeps chatting with a program that imitates his wife. While we teach machines to talk, how did we learn? Trevor Cox, professor of acoustic engineering at the University of Salford, takes up that question in his book, which Er Mu calls the Game of Thrones of acoustics, and, after getting in touch with Cox, this post launches a Chinese translation of it.

The translated introduction begins in December 1877, when Thomas Edison recorded and played back “Mary Had a Little Lamb.” Before the phonograph, speech existed only live; afterwards, how something was said could be kept as well as what was said. Cox recounts the phonograph’s London debut at the Royal Institution in 1878, his own recording of a line by Tennyson on a phonograph there, and how recording and amplification changed speaking and singing, from Henry Irving to David Morrissey, from Adelina Patti to Amy Winehouse. He divides the history of talking into three eras: animal calls, language, and technology that carries one voice to millions. Now AI lets us talk with machines, as in the chatbot Eugenia Kuyda built to keep talking with her late friend Roman Mazurenko. The book asks how we evolved to speak and listen, how children learn to talk, and how technology is changing conversation.

Translated into Chinese by Er Mu from the introduction to Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking: Human Conversation from the Neanderthals to Artificial Intelligence (2018). About the book.
